x: John Milne, who built an early horizontal seismograph, is called the father of modern seismology. Richter devised the magnitude scale, and Wegener proposed continental drift.
t: Match each scientist to his contribution.

x: Option D is incorrect: Zone III (moderate, intensity VII) has a zone factor of 0.16, not 0.24. The factors are 0.10, 0.16, 0.24 and 0.36 for Zones II to V.
t: Recall the zone factors 0.10, 0.16, 0.24 and 0.36.

x: Both are true: the 2001 Bhuj earthquake was a turning point because, with the 2004 tsunami, it pushed India toward the DM Act, 2005. R explains A.
t: Ask whether the outcome explains the 'turning point'.

x: NCS gives real-time quake monitoring, NDMA sets policy guidelines, IS 1893 covers quake-resistant design, and NDRF does specialist search and rescue. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Match each body to its role.

x: All four are correct: the focus is the origin underground, the epicentre is directly above it, intensity is measured on the Mercalli scale, and India has four seismic zones (II to V).
t: Recall the earthquake basics.

x: Both are true: an earthquake is a geological disaster, not an atmospheric one like a cyclone.
t: Sort hazards into geological and atmospheric.

x: All four are correct: AP lies in Zones II and III, and Zones V, IV and III cover the regions listed.
t: Recall the seismic zone map.

x: Option C is incorrect: most of peninsular India is stable and falls in Zone II. Zone V covers the North-East, the Himalayan belt, Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
t: Recall the seismic zone map.

x: The Assam quake struck in 1897, Kangra 1905, Bihar–Nepal 1934 and Assam–Tibet 1950. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Arrange the quakes in time order.

x: All four are correct: the 1897 Assam quake (8.1) was among the first well-studied great quakes, and the 1905 Kangra quake (7.8) killed about 20,000 people.
t: Recall the early great quakes.

x: All four are correct: the 1934 Bihar–Nepal quake (8.1) devastated the Gangetic plains, and the 1950 Assam–Tibet quake (8.6) was one of the largest ever recorded.
t: Recall the great quakes.

x: Both are true: the 1967 Koyna quake was reservoir-induced, and its magnitude was 6.3. Its magnitude does not explain its cause, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a size explains a cause.

x: Both are true: the Latur (Killari) earthquake struck in 1993 with a magnitude of 6.2.
t: Recall the Latur quake.

x: All four are correct: Latur (1993) killed about 10,000, Bhuj (2001) was 7.7, Sikkim (2011) 6.9, and Nepal–Gorkha (2015) 7.8.
t: Recall the recent quakes.

x: Both are true: the Sikkim quake hit the Himalayan region, and the 2015 Gorkha quake also hit Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.
t: Recall the recent quakes.

x: Both are true: the National Building Code has seismic provisions, and seismic microzonation maps risk in cities such as Delhi and Guwahati. One tool does not explain the other, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether two tools explain each other.

x: A tsunami is a series of large waves caused by a sudden movement of the sea floor that displaces a huge volume of water. Wind and rain do not cause it.
t: Recall the definition of a tsunami.

x: Both are true: a tsunami is a natural disaster, and the word is Japanese ('harbour wave'). Where the word comes from does not explain the classification, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a word's origin explains a fact.

x: The focus is where a quake starts, the epicentre is the point above it, the Mercalli scale measures intensity, and the seismograph records shaking. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Match each term to its meaning.

x: Option C is incorrect: the International Tsunami Information Centre is in Honolulu. Hyderabad hosts INCOIS and India's tsunami warning centre.
t: Discriminate the international centre from the Indian one.

x: All three are correct: remote sensing, GIS and satellite data are used to map tsunami and coastal risk.
t: Recall the mapping tools.

x: The order is the International Day for DR (1989), the IDNDR decade (1990), the Yokohama conference (1994) and Sendai (2015). The answer is A, B, C, D.
t: Arrange the milestones in time order.

x: All five were badly hit by the 2004 tsunami: Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Kerala, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
t: Recall the areas hit in 2004.

x: All seven are correct: earthquakes are the usual cause, and undersea or land impacts, landslides, volcanoes, explosions and meteor strikes can also cause tsunamis.
t: Recall the triggers of tsunamis.

x: A tsunami can strike at any time of day or night, as it depends on sea-floor movement, not time or season.
t: Watch for 'only'.

x: All four are tsunami effects: stripping beaches, uprooting plantations, flooding far inland, and damaging life and property.
t: Recall the effects of a tsunami.

x: As a tsunami nears shallow water it slows down and grows much taller.
t: Recall how a tsunami changes near shore.

x: Both are true: tsunami waves reach the coast and cause flooding and destruction.
t: Recall the effects of a tsunami.

x: The Indian Ocean tsunami struck on 26 December 2004, after a 9.1 quake off Sumatra.
t: Recall the tsunami date.

x: As given, India had over 12,000 confirmed deaths, 5,640 people unaccounted for, and damage of over ₹11,000 crore (about US$2.56 billion). The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Match each figure to its item.

x: Both are true: ITEWC stands for Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre, and it sits at INCOIS, Hyderabad.
t: Recall what ITEWC stands for.

x: Both are true: an undersea earthquake can cause a tsunami, and the study of earthquakes is seismology.
t: Recall the basics.

x: Tsunami Day is 5 November, the DRR Day 13 October, Sendai is about disaster risk reduction, and GIS works with spatial data. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Match each item to its detail.

x: The International Nuclear Event Scale (IAEA, 1990) rates nuclear and radiological events from 0 to 7.
t: Match each scale to its hazard.

x: Option B is incorrect: the Beaufort scale rates wind force from 0 to 12. Quake intensity from I to XII uses the Modified Mercalli or MSK-64 scale.
t: Match each scale to its hazard.

x: Both are true: the moment magnitude scale is preferred for big quakes and is the modern standard. Being the standard does not explain why it suits big quakes (Richter saturates at high values), so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a status explains a technical reason.

x: Saffir-Simpson rates hurricane winds, Fujita tornadoes, Richter quake energy, and Beaufort general wind force. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Match each scale to its hazard.

x: I, II and III are correct: the IMD's Indian scale runs from depression to super cyclonic storm, and Saffir-Simpson runs Categories 1–5. IV is false because quake intensity I–XII is MMI or MSK-64.
t: Match each scale to its hazard.

x: Fujita runs F0/EF0 to F5/EF5, Richter was devised in 1935, moment magnitude is written Mw, and the Modified Mercalli scale is MMI. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Match each scale to its detail.

x: All four are correct: Fujita rates tornadoes, and the Richter and moment magnitude scales are logarithmic, Richter usually running from 1 to 10.
t: Recall the features of each scale.

x: Both are true: the Mercalli scale rates intensity by what people see and the damage done, which is why it is based on observed effects. R explains A.
t: Ask whether the method explains the measure.

x: The MSK-64 intensity scale is used in India and much of Europe. MMI is used mainly in the USA.
t: Discriminate MSK-64 from MMI.
